strengths: Targets a relevant and challenging problem: visual analogy completion with demonstration-based editing.
Proposes a simple and well-motivated architecture: a learnable basis of LoRAs plus a CLIP-based router that dynamically composes a task-specific LoRA.
Provides a fairly broad empirical study, including four baselines, automatic VLM-based metrics, a user study, and ablations on capacity, activation, encoder input layout, and encoder choice.
Qualitative results show diverse edits and several cases where the method outperforms prior visual-analogy approaches.
Implementation details, dataset sourcing, and evaluation protocols are mostly documented, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: LoRA bases, mixture-of-LoRA experts, and input-conditioned routing have been explored before; the application to visual analogy is incremental.

The main comparisons to prior methods are confounded by different base models: the proposed method uses the stronger Flux.1-Kontext, while RelationAdapter, VisualCloze, and EditTransfer are run on Flux.1-Dev.

On the fairest comparison—against a single LoRA of equivalent capacity on the same backbone—the gains are small and inconsistent across metrics (e.g., edit accuracy +0.24, preservation -0.12, LPIPS worse, CLIP directional +0.01), with only ~58% pairwise preference.

The mathematical formulation of the mixed LoRA is questionable: Eq. (2) combines A and B factors separately, which yields a product with cross terms rather than a linear combination of LoRA updates, undermining the 'spanning' claim unless well justified.

The evaluation relies heavily on a custom validation set (540 triplets) and a small user study (33 users, 45 pairs), rather than a standard public benchmark; results may be biased by LLM-generated prompts and community LoRAs used to construct targets.
VLM-based evaluation is not fully validated: human-VLM agreement (66.7%) is below human-human agreement (74.2%), and the reported 89.9% normalization is not a standard measure.
There are minor notation and writing issues (e.g., the LoRA scaling equation uses n/r but then mentions α, and typographical errors), and the limitations/societal-impact discussion is brief.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging task: visual analogy completion, where transformations are specified by image pairs rather than text.

Builds on a strong modern backbone (Flux.1-Kontext) and leverages full triplet conditioning via extended attention, which is a sensible design choice for preserving fine details while using CLIP for routing.
The proposed LoRA-basis plus input-conditioned routing is a reasonable and clearly motivated direction, inspired by prior work on LoRA weight-space interpolation.
Provides several ablations on basis size, rank, activation function, encoder input layout, and alternative image encoders.
Includes both automated VLM-based metrics and a user study, and attempts to validate VLM preference against human preferences.
Qualitative results demonstrate the method can handle a variety of edits and sometimes better copy analogy-specific details than single-LoRA or prior baselines.
Implementation details are mostly clear, including optimizer settings, model choices, and the list of community LoRAs used for out-of-domain evaluation.
The paper discusses limitations, which is useful for contextualizing the scope of the method.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: input-dependent composition of multiple LoRAs is closely related to existing mixture-of-LoRA-expert and conditional LoRA composition methods. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish its technical contribution from these prior approaches.

The term 'basis' is misleading: there is no orthogonality, diversity, or spanning constraint on the learned LoRAs, and no analysis showing that they form a meaningful basis or decompose the transformation space. The method is essentially a learned mixture-of-experts over LoRAs.

Comparisons are confounded by different base models: LoRWeB and the single-LoRA baseline use Flux.1-Kontext, while RelationAdapter, VisualCloze, and EditTransfer are based on Flux.1-Dev. The stronger backbone gives LoRWeB a substantial advantage, undermining the claimed state-of-the-art comparisons.

No evaluation on the official Relation252k test split or a standard visual analogy benchmark. The paper instead constructs a custom validation set using LLM-generated prompts and community LoRAs, making results difficult to compare with prior work and potentially biased.

Quantitative improvements are marginal: against the same-backbone LoRA r=128, pairwise VLM win rate is only 57.9% and user study win rate is 57.6%, with worse preservation (7.87 vs. 7.99) and worse LPIPS (0.31 vs. 0.27). No statistical significance tests are reported.

Crucial ablations are missing: there is no comparison to uniform or random routing, no simple average of all LoRAs, no removal of image b from the router input, and no text-only or prompt-only baseline to isolate the contribution of visual analogy. Thus, the core claim that dynamic composition drives improvement is not directly supported.

The router conditions on b as well as a and a', so the selected LoRA mixture can change for different target images even when the transformation is the same. This may make the transformation inconsistent and is not analyzed or ablated.

The combination rule sums A and B matrices separately, yielding cross terms between different LoRAs rather than a weighted sum of individual LoRA updates. The paper describes this as a linear combination, but the math and behavior are different, and this discrepancy is not justified or studied.

Custom evaluation may favor the proposed method: out-of-domain transformations are built with Flux.1-Kontext community LoRAs, which the method uses, while prior baselines run on Flux.1-Dev. This is not a neutral test of visual analogy generalization.

The VLM-based evaluation is not sufficiently reliable on its own, and the user study is small (33 users, 45 image pairs) with filtering of failed cases that may bias win rates. The reported VLM-human alignment metric is unusual and not clearly established as a validation protocol.

No analysis of the learned basis is provided: the paper does not show routing coefficients, specialization across LoRAs, entropy/usage statistics, or whether different layers select different primitives. Therefore the interpretability and 'space of LoRAs' claims remain unsupported.

The main paper lacks a clear numerical table comparing all methods across all metrics; key numbers are relegated to the appendix (Table S2), which weakens clarity and makes the empirical case harder to evaluate.

There are several presentation issues, including notation errors in Eq. (1) (n/r instead of alpha/r), typos such as 'appraoch', and ambiguous statements about per-layer routing modules and shared encoders.

Computational cost and parameter count are not reported, despite training per-weight LoRA bases, keys, and projections. This raises reproducibility and practicality concerns for a method that already trains on an H100 for 10K steps.
Some qualitative examples appear to rely heavily on the accompanying text prompt, so it is unclear how much of the performance comes from true visual analogy rather than prompt-based editing.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging task: visual analogy completion, where transformations are specified by image pairs rather than text.

The proposed LoRWeB is intuitive and well-motivated: it learns a basis of LoRA adapters and dynamically composes them per analogy using a lightweight encoder/router, avoiding the bottleneck of a single adapter.

The architecture sensibly separates roles: CLIP/ViT features select the LoRA mixture based on the analogy triplet, while extended attention with a 2x2 composite image preserves fine-grained visual detail.

The evaluation is broad for an editing paper: qualitative results, VLM-based metrics, pairwise comparisons, a user study, a custom validation set, and ablations over basis size, rank, activation, encoder layout, and alternative image encoders.

Ablations support several design choices, e.g. larger basis size helps generalization, separate encoding of a, a', and b outperforms a single 2x2 CLIP input, and the reference pair meaningfully affects the output beyond the text prompt.
The paper includes useful reproducibility details in the appendix, promises code/data release, and provides an analysis of VLM-human agreement in the user study.
The results show improved edit accuracy and better preference over several prior analogy/editing baselines, with qualitative examples covering diverse unseen transformations.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate: mixtures/routing over LoRA experts and LoRA weight-space interpolation are already established ideas, and this paper mainly adapts them to visual analogy completion without new theoretical insight.

The comparison to prior visual analogy methods is not fully controlled: three baselines use Flux.1-Dev while LoRWeB uses the stronger Flux.1-Kontext, so gains over prior work may partly reflect the stronger base model rather than the proposed method.

The improvement over the strongest same-base baseline (single LoRA r=128) is modest: 57.9% pairwise VLM preference and 57.6% user preference, with no clear statistical significance testing; the user study also covers only 33 users and 45 image pairs.

Claims such as 'state-of-the-art' and 'significantly improves generalization' are therefore stronger than the evidence fully supports, especially given the small margins over the controlled single-LoRA baseline.

There is little analysis or visualization of the learned LoRA basis and routing coefficients: the paper does not demonstrate that individual basis adapters capture distinct, interpretable transformation primitives or that the learned basis actually spans the analogy space.

The custom validation set is built from generated prompts, Unsplash images, and community Flux.1-Kontext LoRAs; this may introduce biases and is not a standard benchmark, making comparisons less reproducible and potentially favorable to the same base model.

Some implementation details are missing or unclear, including exactly which weight matrices/layers are adapted, the projection module architecture, the guiding edit prompts, and how the user-study filtering of 'no method succeeded' cases was performed.
There is a notation/clarity issue in the LoRA preliminaries: the update formula uses n/r although the text refers to a scaling constant alpha, and Eq. (4) could be written more carefully.
The Tanh activation ablation underperforms dramatically but is left unexplained, and the paper's hypothesis about norm growth is speculative rather than analyzed.

The evaluation relies heavily on CLIP/LPIPS and a single VLM (Gemma-3); these metrics are known to be imperfect proxies for editing quality, and no additional perceptual or diversity metrics are reported.

strengths: The paper proposes a well-motivated and technically sound architecture for visual analogy learning by replacing a single LoRA adapter with a learnable basis of LoRAs and an input-dependent router, enabling task-specific adaptation in a single forward pass without per-sample optimization.

The empirical evaluation is thorough: qualitative comparisons, VLM-based edit-accuracy/preservation metrics, pairwise VLM preference, a user study, and extensive ablations over basis size, rank, activation choice, encoder input layout, and alternative image encoders. The appendix additionally compares to per-sample optimization methods DIA and PairEdit.

The method is practically efficient: inference overhead is only about +3.1% over a standard single LoRA, and it avoids expensive test-time tuning. This makes the approach attractive for real-world editing workflows.

The paper provides useful analyses of prompt vs. reference-pair dependence, sensitivity to non-identical reference pairs, sensitivity to non-Flux-generated images, and failure cases, which gives a balanced view of the method's behavior.
Presentation is generally clear, with informative figures, a readable method section, and implementation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The main quantitative comparison to prior visual-analogy methods is not fully fair: RelationAdapter, VisualCloze, and EditTransfer are based on Flux.1-Dev, while the proposed method uses Flux.1-Kontext, a stronger editing-specific backbone. Improvements over these baselines may therefore reflect the stronger base model rather than the LoRA-basis contribution. The only same-backbone baseline is a single LoRA, against which gains are more modest.

The custom evaluation set may be biased toward Flux.1-Kontext, since many reference pairs are generated by Flux.1-Kontext or community LoRAs trained for it. Although the appendix tests TEdBench examples, the main quantitative conclusions would be stronger with a more neutral benchmark or reimplementations of prior analogy methods on the same backbone.

The claimed LoRA-basis/space interpretation is not deeply analyzed: there is little evidence that the learned basis LoRAs correspond to interpretable transformation primitives, and no comparison to alternative LoRA-composition strategies such as independently trained LoRAs with test-time optimization or other mixture-of-LoRA baselines. This makes the basis component harder to fully assess.

The advantage over a same-capacity single LoRA is small in several metrics (e.g., pairwise VLM and user-study win rates), and the single LoRA sometimes scores better on preservation/LPIPS/CLIP directional metrics. The central claim of significantly improved generalization rests heavily on comparisons to methods with different backbones.

Ablation results show some unexpected and not fully explained behaviors, such as a large drop in edit accuracy when rank is increased, which suggests sensitivity to hyperparameters and possible overfitting. More analysis or mitigation would strengthen the paper.

Reproducibility is somewhat limited: code is only promised via a website rather than included or linked as an artifact, and some evaluation/data details remain appendix-only. Data and model licensing/attribution are mentioned but not accompanied by broader impact or misuse discussion.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant task—visual analogy completion—and proposes a sensible dynamic LoRA composition framework.
Method is clearly described and easy to follow, with useful diagrams and implementation details.
Evaluation includes qualitative comparisons, automated metrics, a user study, ablations, efficiency analysis, and failure cases.
Shows some improvements over a same-backbone LoRA baseline in pairwise VLM/user preference and better preservation, while inference overhead is small (+3.1%).
The paper discusses limitations such as non-identical reference pairs and failure cases, which is helpful.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the core mechanism is an input-dependent mixture of LoRA experts/router, closely related to existing MoE-LoRA and LoRA-composition work; the application to visual analogy is incremental and lacks deeper analysis of the learned basis.

The main comparison is unfair: RelationAdapter, VisualCloze, and EditTransfer are based on Flux.1-Dev while LoRWeB uses the stronger Flux.1-Kontext backbone, so gains may be due to the base model rather than the proposed method. The only same-backbone baseline is a standard LoRA, which is not a strong prior method.

Quantitative evidence for the state-of-the-art claim is mixed and modest: CLIP directional similarity and LPIPS are not clearly superior, and pairwise VLM preference over the same-backbone r=128 LoRA is only 57.9%.

The custom evaluation set is generated using Flux/Kontext community LoRAs, and for many custom examples there is no ground-truth b', making evaluation reliant on VLM judgments and a relatively small user study (33 users, 45 pairs, after filtering).

Ablation results are noisy and inconsistent: the full model is not best on all metrics (e.g., N=16 often improves CLIP Dir. and pairwise VLM), yet the paper does not adequately justify the final configuration or explain these trends.

The theoretical claim that LoRWeB dramatically increases expressive power is informal; softmax coefficients restrict the mixture to a convex combination of basis LoRAs, so the method does not truly span the full space of rank-Nr LoRAs.

Training details are limited (e.g., single run, 10K steps, no variance across seeds), and the paper does not provide analysis of what the basis LoRAs learn or whether the dynamic routing is semantically meaningful.

strengths: The paper proposes a well-motivated architecture for visual analogy editing: a learnable basis of LoRAs plus a lightweight encoder/router that dynamically composes an input-dependent LoRA in a single forward pass, avoiding test-time optimization.

The method is integrated cleanly with a strong conditional flow model (Flux.1-Kontext), using full reference images via extended attention while reserving CLIP-based features for LoRA selection, which helps balance fine-detail preservation and higher-level analogy semantics.

The experimental evaluation is broad: it includes VLM-based preservation/edit-accuracy metrics, CLIP directional similarity, LPIPS, pairwise VLM comparisons, a human user study, ablations over basis size/rank/activation/encoder choice, efficiency analysis, and failure cases.

Results support the central empirical claim: on the authors' benchmark, LoRWeB outperforms a same-capacity single LoRA and several prior analogy methods, generalizes better to unseen tasks, and is preferred in pairwise evaluations.

The paper is generally clear, provides implementation details, dataset construction details, prompts used for VLM evaluation, and discusses limitations such as reference-pair assumptions and failure cases.
weaknesses: There is a substantive mathematical inconsistency in the LoRA composition formulation. Eq. (2) defines A = sum_i e_i A_i and B = sum_i e_i B_i, but Eq. (5) states ΔW = BA = sum_i e_i (B_i A_i). The product of the summed matrices includes cross terms and has rank at most r, whereas the weighted sum of products can have rank up to Nr. This mismatch undermines the stated rank/capacity argument and the claim that a single rank-r' LoRA is a special case. The implementation and theoretical justification need clarification; if the actual implementation follows Eq. (2), the effective rank is much lower than claimed and the comparison to an r=128 LoRA is misleading.

The comparison to prior visual-analogy methods is confounded: LoRWeB uses Flux.1-Kontext, a stronger editing backbone, while several baselines use Flux.1-Dev. The same-backbone single-LoRA comparison is more informative, but the paper's 'state-of-the-art' claim over prior methods may be inflated by the stronger base model. Baselines should ideally be adapted to the same backbone or the claims should be qualified.

The evaluation relies heavily on a custom benchmark, partly constructed with prompts derived from Relation252k training prompts and with reference edits generated by Flux or community LoRAs. This may bias results toward the proposed method and does not replace a standard, neutral benchmark. The unavailability of the full Relation252k test split is acknowledged, but the custom set design still limits comparability.

There is little direct analysis of the learned LoRA basis: no visualization or measurement of which basis LoRAs are selected for which transformations, whether they specialize semantically, how routing entropy behaves, or whether interpolations between basis elements are meaningful. The 'spanning the analogy space' claim is therefore supported mainly indirectly through downstream scores.

Ablations show that increasing rank or basis size can hurt performance, which the authors attribute to overfitting, but this is not investigated in depth. Scaling behavior and optimization stability remain unclear.

The user study and VLM evaluation are useful but modest in scale: the user study covers 45 image pairs and the pairwise win rate against the same-backbone r=128 LoRA is only 57.9%, which is a relatively small margin. VLM-human agreement is also below user-user agreement, so automated metrics should be interpreted cautiously.

The softmax routing restricts coefficients to be non-negative and sum to one, which may limit the expressiveness of the composed LoRA space; alternatives such as Tanh are tested but not fully explored. This is a design choice that deserves more investigation.

There are minor clarity/reference issues (e.g., the LLM used for prompt degradation is referenced oddly as [20], and some equations/figure descriptions could be tightened), though these are not central to the scientific case.
